opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I read that frontier is that a lot of the movement you see, especially at the low-cost end, is really distillation progress showing up in disguise. When you look at those plots, the frontier models on the top right keep pushing capability, but the really striking thing is how fast the curve shifts left. Something that cost you a frontier-model price a year ago, you can now get from a model that's maybe an order of magnitude cheaper. And a big chunk of that isn't because someone discovered a fundamentally better small architecture. It's because we've gotten much better at transferring what the big model knows into the small one.

The intuition I like is that the large model is doing the hard work of discovery. It's figuring out the structure in the data, what reasoning patterns actually work, how to solve these problems. Once that exists, the small model doesn't have to rediscover all of it from raw pretraining data. It can learn from the teacher's distributions, from its samples, from its reasoning traces. So the teacher has effectively already paid the exploration cost, and the student is just paying for compression. Compression is a lot cheaper than discovery.

What's changed over the last couple of years is that distillation isn't just matching logits on a fixed dataset anymore. Some of the work we did on on-policy distillation, generalized knowledge distillation, was about this: if the student only ever trains on teacher-generated sequences, there's a train–test mismatch, because at inference time the student is conditioning on its own mistakes. If you let the student generate and then have the teacher give feedback on those student-generated tokens, you close that gap. That turns out to matter a lot, especially for reasoning, where errors compound over long sequences. You can think of it as a dense-reward version of RL, where the teacher gives a signal at every token instead of a single sparse reward at the end.

So when I look at the Pareto frontier, I see two forces. The top keeps moving up because of scale, better RL, better data. And then distillation acts like a ratchet that pulls everything down the cost axis shortly after. The gap between when a capability appears at the frontier and when it's available cheaply has been shrinking.

The caveat is that distillation is bounded by the teacher. You're mostly not getting a student that surpasses the teacher on the things the teacher is good at, at least not without some extra signal like verification or RL on top. And there's a capacity question: some capabilities, especially broad knowledge, seem to need parameters, so they compress less gracefully than narrow reasoning skills. Small models can get surprisingly good at math or code because those are relatively compact procedures, but long-tail factual knowledge is harder to squeeze in.

So my summary would be: the frontier tells you about two kinds of progress at once. The upper envelope is about discovering new capabilities, and the leftward shift is largely about distillation getting better at compressing them. Both are moving, but in some ways the compression side is moving faster, which is why it feels like intelligence keeps getting cheaper every few months.

r001.rationale: It describes capability appearing at the frontier, followed by distillation making it cheaper shortly after, and frames these as two forces moving the frontier.

r002.rationale: It links a leftward shift in cost to distillation, but does not interpret a gentler frontier slope as evidence of better distillation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I like to think about it is that there are really two different frontiers moving at once, and people tend to conflate them.

There's the frontier of what's possible at all — the biggest model, the most compute, what's the best capability you can get if you don't care about cost. That frontier moves when you get new pretraining scale, new RL recipes, new data. And then there's this second thing, which is: for a fixed capability level, how cheap can you get it? And that second curve is where distillation lives.

What's been striking to me is how fast that second curve moves. If you look at a capability that was frontier-only, say, eighteen months ago — something you needed the biggest model to do — today you can usually get it in a model that's five, ten, sometimes fifty times cheaper to serve. And the mechanism for most of that is distillation in one form or another. You have a strong teacher, you generate a lot of data from it, maybe you do rejection sampling or you use some verifier to filter, and you train a smaller student on that. The student doesn't have to discover the capability; it just has to absorb it.

So the way I read the Pareto frontier is that the frontier model does the expensive exploration, and distillation is the mechanism that pushes the whole curve down and to the left afterward. It's almost like a lag: the big model finds the capability, and then there's some delay, and then the small model catches up at a fraction of the cost. And one of the interesting questions in the field right now is how short that lag can get. For some capabilities it's really short — the small model is almost as good a couple of months later. For other things, especially stuff that requires a lot of reasoning or world knowledge, the gap is stickier.

The other thing I'd say is that distillation progress is a bit under-appreciated because it's not glamorous. Nobody writes a headline about a model getting three times cheaper. But from a deployment standpoint, that's often the thing that actually matters — whether you can afford to run this in a product, whether you can run it on-device, whether it fits a latency budget. So when I look at the frontier, I'm honestly as excited by how fast the cheap end is moving as by how far out the expensive end is pushing.

And there's a feedback loop too, which I think people are starting to appreciate. Cheaper models mean you can sample more, run more verification, do more search at inference time. So distillation isn't just about compressing a fixed capability — it's also what makes the next round of test-time compute methods economically viable. The small model becomes a tool for making the big model better, and vice versa. That interplay is, to me, the most interesting part of where the frontier is right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes capability growth and efficiency improvements as two frontiers moving at once, but does not characterize progress as an alternating search between them.

r002.rationale: It says distillation pushes the curve down and left, but does not interpret a gentler frontier slope as evidence of better distillation.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as asking: for a given inference cost, what’s the best capability you can get? The Pareto frontier is the set of models where you can’t get more capability without paying more, or pay less without giving up some capability.

Distillation is a way to push that frontier outward. You take a more capable teacher and try to transfer its behavior into a cheaper student. If the student reaches a level of performance that previously required a much more expensive model, that’s meaningful progress—even if it doesn’t beat the teacher.

The distinction I’d make is between moving along the frontier and actually improving it. Making a model smaller and less capable might just move you along the existing curve. Preserving more capability at that smaller size shifts the curve. And you have to account for the inference setup: if the student needs substantially more generated tokens to get the same answer, parameter count alone doesn’t tell you whether you’ve reduced cost.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes moving along the frontier from shifting it outward, but does not describe progress as an alternating search between increasing capability and improving efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret a gentler frontier slope as evidence of better distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to look at it is: for a given level of capability, how much does it cost to deliver that capability? Or, if you fix the cost, how capable a model can you get? The Pareto frontier is the set of models where you can’t improve one of those dimensions without giving something up on the other.

Distillation is a way to push that frontier outward. You take a more capable teacher and use it to train a cheaper student, and the question is how much of the teacher’s capability you can preserve. You don’t necessarily need the student to beat the teacher for that to be meaningful progress. If it gets close at substantially lower inference cost, that’s a very useful improvement.

The caveat is that capability has to be measured on the tasks you actually care about. Matching the teacher on a narrow benchmark is different from preserving its breadth. So I’d look at the whole capability–cost curve, rather than just asking whether the distilled model has a higher score.

r001.rationale: The response describes trading off capability and cost and pushing the frontier outward, but does not describe progress as a search that alternates between increasing capability and improving efficiency.

r002.rationale: The response does not interpret a gentler frontier slope as indicating better distillation.
